clips.send: Inertia (green arrow). Keeps it moving straight ahead. Inertia is an object’s tendency to keep moving in a straight line at the same speed. The green arrow shows which way the satellite is moving right now; the dashed line shows where it would go if gravity switched off. In space there is almost no air to slow it down, so it does not need an engine to keep going. Inertia + gravity together make the curved path of an orbit. Orbit equals inertia (straight ahead) + gravity (toward the center).

clips.send: Gravity (red arrow). Always pulls toward the center. The red arrow always points to the center of the planet. It is longer when the satellite is closer (gravity is stronger) and shorter when it is farther away. Doubling the planet’s mass doubles the pull. Gravity keeps changing the direction of the motion, bending the straight path into a curve. Gravity equals the steering force that bends the path.

clips.send: Satellite (cannonball). Moving sideways while falling. Two things decide its path: its sideways motion (inertia) and gravity pulling it toward the planet. From this launch height (about 1,100 km up), about 7.3 km/s gives a circular orbit around an Earth-mass planet. The International Space Station orbits at about 7.7 km/s and circles Earth every 90 minutes. Faster than about 10.3 km/s from here, gravity can no longer bring it back: it escapes. Too slow, falls. Just right, orbits. Too fast, escapes.

clips.send: Newton’s mountain. A thought experiment from 1687. Isaac Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain so tall it pokes above the air, so there is no air resistance. A slow cannonball curves down and hits the ground. Faster balls land farther away, because the planet’s surface curves away beneath them. Fast enough, the ball falls around the planet forever and never lands: it is in orbit! An orbit is falling while always missing the ground.

clips.send: It fell back down. Too slow to orbit. Gravity pulled the ball down before it could get all the way around the planet. A faster launch lands farther away, because the ground curves away below it. On a planet with more mass you would need an even faster launch. Not fast enough sideways, gravity wins.

clips.send: Planet (Earth). Its mass makes the gravity. Every object with mass pulls on every other object. That pull is gravity. More mass means stronger gravity. Try the planet-mass slider: the planet stays the same size and only its mass changes. Gravity pulls toward the center of the planet, which is why “down” points a different way in Georgia and in Australia. Gravity gets weaker with distance, but it never completely switches off. More mass, more pull. More distance, less pull.

clips.send: 引力（红色箭头）。总是指向中心。红色箭头始终指向行星的中心。卫星离得越近，箭头越长（引力越强）；离得越远，箭头越短。行星质量加倍，拉力也加倍。引力不断改变运动的方向，把直线路径弯成曲线。引力就像“方向盘”，把路径掰弯。

clips.send: 行星（地球）。它的质量产生引力。任何有质量的物体都会吸引其他物体，这种吸引就是引力。质量越大，引力越强。试试“行星质量”滑块：行星大小不变，只改变质量。引力指向行星的中心，所以佐治亚州和澳大利亚的人“向下”的方向不同。引力随距离增大而减弱，但永远不会完全消失。质量越大，引力越大；距离越远，引力越小。

clips.send: 牛顿的高山。1687 年的思想实验。艾萨克·牛顿想象在一座高到伸出大气层的山顶上放一门大炮，这样就没有空气阻力。慢速的炮弹沿弧线下落，撞到地面。速度越快，落得越远，因为行星表面在它下方向下弯曲。速度足够快时，炮弹会永远绕着行星“下落”而落不了地：它进入了轨道！轨道就是一直在下落，却总是落不到地面。
clips.text: 牛顿的高山. 1687 年的思想实验. 艾萨克·牛顿想象在一座高到伸出大气层的山顶上放一门大炮，这样就没有空气阻力。. 慢速的炮弹沿弧线下落，撞到地面。. 速度越快，落得越远，因为行星表面在它下方向下弯曲。. 速度足够快时，炮弹会永远绕着行星“下落”而落不了地：它进入了轨道！. 轨道就是一直在下落，却总是落不到地面。

clips.send: 卫星（炮弹）。一边横向运动，一边下落。决定它路径的有两样东西：横向运动（惯性）和把它拉向行星的引力。从这个高度（约 1100 千米）发射，速度约 7.3 千米/秒时，它会绕地球质量的行星做圆周运动。国际空间站的速度约为 7.7 千米/秒，每 90 分钟绕地球一圈。从这里发射，速度超过约 10.3 千米/秒时，引力就拉不回它了：它会逃逸。太慢，落地；刚好，绕行；太快，逃逸。

clips.send: 它落回地面了。速度太慢，无法绕行。炮弹还没绕行星一圈，就被引力拉回了地面。发射得越快，落得越远，因为地面在它下方向下弯曲。在质量更大的行星上，需要更快的发射速度。横向速度不够快，引力获胜。

clips.send: 惯性（绿色箭头）。让它保持直线前进。惯性是物体保持原来的速度、沿直线运动的性质。绿色箭头表示卫星此刻运动的方向；虚线表示如果没有引力，它会沿哪条直线飞走。太空中几乎没有空气让它减速，所以不需要发动机也能一直运动。惯性 + 引力共同造成了弯曲的轨道。轨道 等于 惯性（向前直走）+ 引力（拉向中心）。
